sets.t: Learning a musical instrument as an adult
sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện học nhạc cụ khi đã lớn
sp: I'd always assumed that if I took one lesson a week, I'd be playing simple songs within a couple of months. My teacher was very polite about it, but after the third lesson she asked how much I'd practised, and the honest answer was about ten minutes. It turns out that twenty minutes a day, every day, is the minimum. Once I accepted that, things improved, but it took me a while to stop expecting results without the work.

My daughter started the violin at school, and I used to sit in the car during her lessons, scrolling through my phone. One day her teacher suggested I join in, just for fun. Now we practise together most evenings, and we've even played a duet at my mother's birthday. We were never particularly close when she was younger, and this has given us something that's just ours.

I work in a hospital emergency department, so my days are pretty intense. I took up the drums because a friend said hitting things would be good for me, and he was right. After a difficult shift, half an hour of drumming clears my head in a way nothing else does. I'm not especially talented, and I'll never play in a band, but that isn't the point. It's my way of letting go of the day.

I signed up for group guitar classes at the community centre, and when I walked in on the first evening, everyone else was about fifteen. I nearly turned round and went home. I felt so out of place, being the oldest by thirty years. But the teenagers were lovely. They'd show me chords and laugh at my jokes, even the bad ones. By the end of the course, I'd stopped noticing the age difference at all.

I live in a very small flat, and I travel a lot for work, so a piano was never an option. I chose the ukulele because it's light enough to take anywhere. I've played it in hotel rooms all over the world, quietly, so I don't disturb anyone. Some of my friends think it's a toy rather than a real instrument, but I've learned to play some quite complicated pieces on it.

tasks.q: What does each speaker say about learning the instrument?
o: It helped me deal with pressure at work.
At first I felt awkward about being much older than the others.
I had to change teachers to make progress.
I underestimated how much practice was needed.
It brought me closer to a family member.
I gave up for a while but later started again.
Playing in front of other people was the hardest part.
I chose my instrument because it was easy to carry.

sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện chuyển đến thành phố mới
sp: When I got the job offer in the capital, the salary looked enormous compared with what I'd been earning. What nobody told me was that rent would take more than half of it. My first flat was a single room above a laundry, and by the end of each month I was living on noodles. It took me nearly two years to save enough to move somewhere decent.

I didn't know a soul when I arrived, and I mostly worked from home, so I could easily have gone weeks without talking to anyone. Then I saw a poster for a running club that met in the park on Sunday mornings. I'm a terrible runner, but the people were great, and most of my closest friends here are from that club.

My partner had been offered a research post at the university, and it was too good an opportunity for her to turn down. I'd lived in the same town all my life, so for me the move was a big step. I spent the first few months looking for work and feeling a bit lost, if I'm honest, but I've found a job I enjoy now.

People had warned me that big-city people are cold and unfriendly, so I expected to be ignored. In fact, on my first day, my neighbour knocked on the door with a plate of cakes, and the man at the corner shop learned my name within a week. I'm not saying everyone is like that, but it certainly wasn't what I'd been led to believe.

The first month was miserable. It rained constantly, I hated my job, and I had a ticket home booked for the end of the month. Then, two days before I was due to leave, my manager moved me to a different team, and suddenly everything changed. I cancelled the ticket, and that was six years ago.

tasks.q: What does each speaker say about moving to the city?
o: I found it hard to make friends at work.
The cost of living was higher than I'd expected.
A hobby helped me meet people.
I missed the food from home.
I often got lost at first.
I moved because of my partner's job.
I was surprised by how friendly people were.
I nearly went back home in the first month.

sets.t: A job they did as students
sets.tvi: Năm người kể về việc làm thêm thời sinh viên
sp: I worked at the complaints desk of a department store during the holidays. Some days people would shout at me about things that had nothing to do with me, like the weather or the parking. I learned not to take it personally, to listen first and then offer something practical. Those skills have been surprisingly useful in every job I've had since.

I spent a summer picking fruit on a farm. I thought it would be a relaxing way to earn some money outdoors, but by the end of the first day my back was aching and my hands were covered in scratches. You're bending over for eight hours in the sun. I was fitter than I'd ever been by the end, though.

I was studying law, and I took a part-time job as a teaching assistant at a primary school, mainly for the money. I didn't expect to enjoy it so much. Seeing a child suddenly understand something was more satisfying than anything in my law books. I finished my degree, but then I trained as a teacher, and I've never regretted it.

I had two jobs while I was at university, one in a café and one doing deliveries, as well as my studies. At first it was chaos. I missed deadlines and once fell asleep in a lecture. Eventually I started planning every week on a big calendar on my wall, and that habit has stayed with me. I still can't work without a plan.

I worked nights at a hotel reception desk. It was quiet most of the time, and the other receptionist, a woman from Brazil, and I used to talk for hours about everything. That was twenty years ago. She came to my wedding, I went to hers, and we still call each other every month.

tasks.q: What does each speaker say about the job?
o: It taught me to organise my time.
I was treated unfairly by my employer.
It led me to choose a different career.
I earned more than I had expected.
I learned how to deal with difficult customers.
I made a friend for life.
It was harder physically than I'd imagined.
I only did it because my parents insisted.

sets.tvi: Năm người kể vì sao đi làm tình nguyện
sp: When my father lost his job, it was a food bank that kept us going for months, and I never forgot the volunteers there, how they treated us with dignity. So when I was earning again, it felt only right to give something back. What surprised me was how complicated the issue of food poverty is. I'd assumed it was mostly about people being unemployed, but many of the people we help have jobs; they just don't earn enough. That's changed how I talk about it.

I'd just retired, and frankly, I was climbing the walls. After forty years of busy working days, I had nothing to fill the hours. A neighbour mentioned that the hospital needed drivers to take patients to appointments, so I signed up. I've always been a rather impatient person, as my children would tell you, but sitting in waiting rooms for hours has taught me to slow down. I hardly recognise myself.

I needed a placement for my social work degree, it was compulsory, and I ended up at a homeless shelter. I went in feeling rather pleased with myself for helping. What struck me, though, was how much luck had been on my side all along: a family to fall back on, a safety net I'd never even noticed. I'm still volunteering there, two years after the placement ended.

I'd moved to the city for work and didn't know anyone. A colleague suggested the conservation group that spends weekends clearing rubbish from the river, and I went along mostly hoping to make some friends. What I hadn't expected was how much I'd learn: how to use the tools properly, how to identify plants, even how to repair a small boat. Those are things I'd never have picked up in an office.

I saw a documentary about adult literacy and was shocked by how many people struggle to read a simple form. I volunteered as a reading tutor the following week. At first I was terrified of the group sessions, because I'd always hated speaking in front of people, but having to explain things clearly to a room of adults has done more for my nerves than any course could. I've even given a talk at the library.

tasks.q: Task 1: Why did each speaker start volunteering?
o: to gain experience for a future career
because a friend kept persuading them
to repay help they had once received
because they had too much free time
to meet people after moving
because of a sense of guilt
because their course required it
because of something they saw on television

tasks.q: Task 2: What has each speaker gained from volunteering?
o: practical skills
a sense of belonging
more patience
a better relationship with their family
a more realistic view of the problem
a new career direction
confidence in speaking to groups
an awareness of their own advantages

sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện tự mở doanh nghiệp
sp: It started with a few candles I made for friends at Christmas. They kept asking for more, and then friends of friends did, until my kitchen was full of wax. When I finally turned it into a business, the hardest thing by far was deciding what to charge. Charge too little and you're working for nothing; charge too much and people walk away. I changed my prices four times in the first year.

When the factory closed, two hundred of us lost our jobs on the same day. I'd been a mechanic there for fifteen years, so I opened a small repair workshop with my redundancy money. The work itself has been fine. What I wasn't prepared for was being on my own all day. At the factory there was always someone to have a laugh with. Now it's just me and the radio.

I live in a town full of elderly people, and I noticed there was nobody offering to help them with technology: setting up phones, video-calling grandchildren, that kind of thing. So I started doing it. Demand has never been the problem. The difficulty is that the big electronics chains have noticed the same thing and started offering similar help in their shops. A small business like mine simply can't match their size.

I'd worked for the same manager for six years, and he never listened to a single idea I had. In the end I thought: if I'm going to work this hard, it might as well be for myself. So I started a small catering company. The clients pay well, but often sixty or ninety days after the event, while I have to pay for food and staff immediately. There were months when I genuinely didn't know if I could pay the rent.

I've got three young children, and an office job with fixed hours just wasn't working any more. So I set up as a freelance translator. I can choose when I work, which is wonderful. The downside is that the office is the kitchen table, and the children don't understand that when I'm at the laptop, I'm not available. Clients have heard a toddler screaming during video calls more times than I'd like to admit.

tasks.q: Task 1: What led each speaker to start the business?
o: losing their job
noticing a need nobody was meeting
a hobby that grew
wanting more flexible hours
encouragement from a mentor
frustration with a former boss
winning a competition
a family tradition

tasks.q: Task 2: What has been each speaker's biggest difficulty?
o: finding reliable staff
waiting to be paid
competing with large companies
working alone
dealing with regulations
setting the right price
advertising the business
keeping work and family life apart

sets.t: Learning a foreign language as an adult
sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện học ngoại ngữ khi đã lớn
sp: My wife's family is from Seville, and for the first years of our marriage I'd sit at family dinners smiling and understanding nothing. I wanted to be able to joke with her father, not just nod at him. Apps didn't do much for me, to be honest. What changed everything was a weekly conversation evening at a bar near my office. Two hours of talking, making mistakes, and nobody minding.

After I retired, my doctor said something about keeping the brain busy, and learning a language seemed more interesting than crosswords. I chose Italian. The grammar books were hopeless for me; I'd forget everything by the next day. Then my granddaughter lent me some of her picture books. Simple sentences, lots of repetition, and pictures to help. I'm now on to proper novels, slowly.

At school my French teacher told me I had no ear for languages, and I believed her for twenty years. Then one day I thought, why should she have the last word? I started learning Japanese, of all things. I write a few lines every evening about my day, in Japanese, and once a week a language partner online corrects them. Seeing my mistakes in writing helps them stick.

I got hooked on a Korean drama during lockdown, and after months of reading subtitles I wanted to understand it properly. I started picking up phrases almost by accident. Then I switched the subtitles to Korean as well as the sound, so I could see and hear the words at the same time. That's been far more useful than any textbook.

My company was opening an office in Brazil, and the manager's job there required Portuguese. I had six months. I'm too shy for conversation groups, so I did something that probably looks a bit mad: I described everything I was doing out loud, in Portuguese, while I cooked, cleaned and drove to work. It forced me to find the words I was missing. I got the job.

tasks.q: Task 1: Why did each speaker start learning the language?
o: to communicate with their partner's family
to get a better job
to read literature in the original
because of a trip they were planning
to keep their mind active
because of a television series
to help their children with homework
to prove someone wrong

tasks.q: Task 2: What has helped each speaker most?
o: a private tutor

a regular conversation group
watching with subtitles

writing a daily diary

sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện đổi nghề giữa đời
sp: I spent fifteen years in advertising, much of it selling things to children that their parents couldn't really afford. For a long time I told myself that everybody does it, but the justification wore thinner every year, until one campaign for a sugary cereal felt like the last straw. I retrained as a primary teacher. The work is infinitely more rewarding, but I won't pretend the salary isn't a shock. We've sold the second car, and holidays are camping trips now.

A minor heart problem at forty-four, nothing dramatic in the end, but it made me take stock. I'd always loved woodwork, so I enrolled on a furniture-making course. What I hadn't bargained for was how hard it is to be bad at something. I'd forgotten what it feels like not to know how to do anything. Cutting a straight line took me weeks, and I went home most evenings feeling about twelve years old.

I was a corporate lawyer, and I'd never considered anything else until I got chatting to a stranger on a delayed train who turned out to run a vineyard. By the time we reached London I'd more or less decided. I now work for a winemaker in Portugal, and the hardest adjustment has been the hierarchy. My supervisor is twenty-six, and she's perfectly entitled to tell me how to do my job, which she does without hesitation.

Once our youngest left for university, the house was suddenly very quiet, and I realised I'd organised my whole life around school runs and timetables. I left my job at the bank to try freelance illustration. Nobody warned me how disorientating it is to have no one telling you when to start or stop. Some days I achieve a great deal; others simply dissolve into coffee and good intentions.

I'd wanted to be a nurse since I was a child, but my family needed me to earn money, so I went into insurance and stayed for twenty years. When the mortgage was finally paid off, there was nothing stopping me any more. What genuinely surprised me was how some old friends reacted, as though I'd announced I was joining a cult. A few have drifted away. The ones who stayed have been wonderful.

tasks.q: Task 1: What prompted each speaker to change career?
o: a health scare

tasks.q: Task 2: What has each speaker found hardest since the change?

sets.tvi: Năm người kể chuyện sống ở nước ngoài
sp: In my own language I'm the person who makes the jokes at dinner, but in German I was reduced to someone who could only discuss the weather and train times. It was oddly painful, feeling that people were meeting a duller version of me. Eight years on, I'm fluent, and the strange thing is that when I go back to Lisbon now, I feel like a visitor there too. I'm no longer certain which place I'd call home.

Nothing prepared me for the paperwork. To open a bank account I needed an address; to rent a flat I needed a bank account. It took four months, three visits to the same office and a great deal of patience to break the circle. Ironically, it's made me far more appreciative of the system back home, which I used to complain about constantly. At least there, the forms are online and somebody answers the phone.

In Brazil, a dinner invitation for eight o'clock means people start arriving around half past nine, and I spent my first months sitting alone in tidy flats wondering whether I'd got the day wrong. I've relaxed about that now. What I hadn't expected was to see my own country differently. Back in the Netherlands, we pride ourselves on being honest, but I now realise how blunt we can sound. My Brazilian friends find us quite alarming.

During the week, work kept me busy, but Sundays in Seoul were long and silent. Everybody seemed to be with family, and I'd wander round shopping centres just to be among people. Living there made me realise how much I'd taken my village for granted: the way neighbours drop in uninvited, the endless gossip at the shop. I used to find it suffocating; now I miss it.

Coming from Kerala to Norway, I'd prepared myself for the cold, but not for the dark. In December the sun barely rises. I took vitamin pills, bought a special lamp and gradually adjusted. Norwegians repair things, share things and recycle with an almost religious seriousness, and since living here I can't visit my family without noticing how much we throw away. I bite my tongue, mostly.

tasks.q: Task 1: What did each speaker find hardest at first?
o: the bureaucracy

the food

sets.tvi: Năm người kể về một lần thất bại trong nghề
sp: As a young scientist I published a result I was very proud of, and then two other labs tried to reproduce it and couldn't. It turned out the effect came from a contaminated batch of chemicals. I felt humiliated at the time, but it made me a much better researcher. Now, whenever a result looks too neat, my first question is what I might be taking for granted.

My first novel was turned down by twenty-three publishers. For a while each rejection felt like a verdict on me as a person, which is absurd when you think about it. What eventually changed was that I began to see the manuscript as a thing I had made, rather than a piece of myself. The book that finally got published was my third, and the rejections that came before it stung far less.

Twenty minutes into the most important concert of my career, the power failed and the stage went dark. I stood there frozen, with eight hundred people waiting. Eventually the orchestra carried on from memory, but I've never forgotten the panic. These days I rehearse for disasters: what we'll do if a string breaks, if a soloist falls ill, if the lights go. It sounds pessimistic, but it's actually what lets me relax on stage.

My business partner and I had been friends since university, and we ran the company together for nine years before it fell apart over money. Looking back, the problems were obvious for at least two years, but I was too proud to admit I couldn't solve them alone. If I'd brought in an adviser, or even just talked to someone honestly, I suspect we'd still be in business, and still be friends.

We spent eighteen months developing a smart water bottle that reminded you to drink. Every investor loved it; every customer ignored it. The few honest reviewers who said it solved a problem nobody had were dismissed by our team as people who didn't get it. They got it perfectly well. Now, when someone tells me an idea won't work, I make myself take the objection seriously before I defend the idea.

o: to ask for help earlier
